metadata.note: The Abraham Lincoln and Ann Rutledge on the Chicago-St. Louis corridor, run by the Alton Railroad and then Gulf, Mobile & Ohio - the historical predecessors of Amtrak's Lincoln Service. Route geometry is taken from the modern Amtrak route's own GTFS-sourced alignment for this corridor (see amtrak.geojson), since the historical train ran the same physical line; where the historical train ran beyond or differently from today's Amtrak route, that is described in the segment notes. Era boundaries follow real, sourced milestones; headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not from real timetables. CORRECTION (2026-08-18): this line originally began in 1935 with the streamlined Abraham Lincoln, which wrongly left the Chicago-St. Louis corridor blank for the entire 19th century. Segments now run back to the Alton & Sangamon's 1852 opening and the 1856 completion of the through line to Chicago. CORRECTION (2026-08-24): the 1971-1978 Amtrak segment has been removed from this feature and redrawn as its own Amtrak-coloured layer, amtrak_abraham_lincoln_ann_rutledge.geojson. It had been asserting Amtrak service under the Alton/GM&O company name and colour, which breaks Rule 4 and Rule 6. This file now covers only the pre-Amtrak era, ending May 1 1971.
metadata.source: Wikipedia (Abraham Lincoln, Alton Railroad, Gulf Mobile and Ohio), american-rails.com
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.geometry_fix: 2026-08-27: four vertices between Alton and Godfrey (indices 12-15) were out of order, so the line ran north to 38.9948, doubled back south to 38.9579 and went north again, revisiting the same spot twice about 100 m apart -- the out-and-back spike described in this repo's tracing notes, and the kind of thing that reads on the map as a real historical quirk when it is only a vertex-ordering error. Reordering them into a monotone progression up the river removed both reversals the spike detector flagged and brought the drawn length from 285.7 to 280.3 miles against the 284 route miles this file's own note documents; the coarse 57-point polyline understates the true length by chording, so 280.3 is the expected figure and 285.7 was 5.4 miles of doubling back. No other vertex was touched. NOTE (CLAUDE.md Rule 2): this trace is still a 57-point approximation of a 284-mile route -- roughly one point every 5 miles -- and has never been real-traced from OSM. The Kansas City lines added the same day in chicago_alton_kansas_city.geojson are traced properly and are much finer.

segments.note: Extended to Bloomington in 1854 as the Chicago & Mississippi and to Joliet in 1855; the Joliet & Chicago Railroad opened in 1856, completing a continuous line from Alton through to Chicago. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: After several bankruptcies and reorganizations the company settled as the Chicago & Alton Railroad by Oct 10 1862, running Chicago-Springfield-Alton-St. Louis for the rest of the century. St. Louis Union Station opened Sept 1 1894 as the world's largest and busiest terminal, its train shed covering 30 tracks serving 22 railroads - the physical proof of how much rail converged here. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Abraham Lincoln was the first streamlined service over the 284-mile Chicago-St. Louis route, calling at Joliet, Bloomington-Normal, Springfield and Alton, run by the Alton Railroad (which dated to 1847). estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Gulf, Mobile & Ohio bought the Alton in 1947, retiring the Alton name; the Abraham Lincoln and its companion the Ann Rutledge carried GM&O's two-tone maroon and yellow livery on this corridor. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable Gulf, Mobile and Ohio operation ended when Amtrak took over on May 1 1971; the Amtrak era of both trains is drawn separately in amtrak_abraham_lincoln_ann_rutledge.geojson.
